title: Maxwell's Demon: Is Information Physical?
question: Could a tiny intelligent being sort molecules to beat the second law of thermodynamics, and what does the answer reveal about the nature of information?
summary: A nineteenth-century thought experiment about a molecule-sorting demon took a century to resolve, and the resolution — that erasing information has an unavoidable energy cost — revealed that information is a physical quantity bound by thermodynamics.
content:
A Demon at the Door

In 1867 James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny being guarding a trapdoor between two chambers of gas at the same temperature. Whenever a fast molecule approached from the left, the demon opened the door; whenever a slow one approached from the right, it did the same. Over time, fast molecules piled up on one side and slow ones on the other: a hot chamber and a cold chamber, created from uniform gas without any work being done. That temperature difference could then run an engine. The demon seemed to break the second law of thermodynamics, the one law physicists trusted above nearly all others.

The Price of Knowing

For decades the paradox resisted resolution. Leo Szilard in 1929 boiled it down to a single-molecule engine and suggested that the act of measurement must cost entropy. Later, Léon Brillouin argued that seeing a molecule requires shining light on it, and the photons carry away the gained entropy. But Charles Bennett showed in the 1980s that measurement can, in principle, be done reversibly and nearly for free. The real cost lies elsewhere.

Landauer's Principle: Forgetting Is Expensive

Rolf Landauer argued in 1961 that erasing one bit of information must dissipate at least kT ln 2 of heat into the environment. A demon has finite memory. To keep sorting molecules forever, it must eventually wipe its records of past measurements, and that erasure produces at least as much entropy as the sorting removed. The second law survives, but only once we count information as a physical quantity with a thermodynamic price. In 2012, experimenters trapping a single colloidal bead in a laser measured heat release approaching the Landauer limit, turning a thought experiment into a laboratory fact.

Information Is Physical

Landauer's slogan, "information is physical," reshaped how physicists think. Entropy in thermodynamics (Boltzmann's count of microstates) and entropy in Claude Shannon's theory of communication (uncertainty about a message) turn out to be not just formally analogous but deeply linked. A bit stored in memory is a constrained physical state; destroying the distinction between 0 and 1 means pushing that constraint out into the world as heat. Modern "information engines" built from single electrons and molecules now extract work from measurements, exactly as Szilard imagined, while paying their bill at erasure time.

Why It Still Matters

The demon's legacy reaches far beyond gases. It frames the ultimate energy limits of computation: today's chips dissipate millions of times more than Landauer's bound per operation, so there is vast room for improvement, and reversible computing aims to dodge the cost by never erasing at all. It informs biology, where molecular machines like kinesin and ion pumps behave like ratchets that harvest fluctuations using fuel and feedback. And it sits at the heart of the black hole information paradox, where the question of whether information can be destroyed collides with quantum theory and gravity. A tiny imaginary gatekeeper ended up revealing that knowledge, memory, and forgetting are woven into the physics of heat.

perspectives.title: Thermodynamics Perspective
perspectives.description: The second law is statistical, not absolute; the demon forces us to ask whether intelligence can exploit fluctuations, and the answer is only by paying an entropy cost elsewhere.

perspectives.title: Information Theory Perspective
perspectives.description: Shannon entropy and Boltzmann entropy are two faces of one idea: missing information about a system's microstate. Landauer's principle is the exchange rate between them.

perspectives.title: Computer Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Every irreversible logical operation, like overwriting a register, has a minimum energy cost, which motivates reversible computing and sets the far horizon of energy-efficient hardware.

perspectives.title: Biological Perspective
perspectives.description: Cells are full of demon-like molecular machines that use measurement and feedback, paid for with ATP, to rectify random thermal motion into directed work.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The long history of failed and partial resolutions shows how a thought experiment can stay productive for 150 years, with each generation locating the hidden cost in a different place.

openQuestions: Does the Landauer bound hold unchanged for quantum memories, where measurement itself disturbs the system?
Can practical reversible computers ever outcompete conventional chips, or will error correction reintroduce the erasure cost?
Is the identification of thermodynamic and informational entropy a deep truth about nature or a useful analogy we have over-trusted?
If information is physical, what physical substrate carries the information that seems to vanish into a black hole?
